snapshot.description: The coal is all but gone. Every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on dubhan, the fuel one Tuathach made from the waste of the mines; the coin is pegged to it, a tithe laid for a war is taken at every pump, and this autumn the first tank-hull went out past the north-western capes under Dubhan's narrow charter while the priests of Manannan prayed the sea shut. Cathal reigns at Cathair dhearg over one hundred and twenty-three shires; nine regiments and four fleets raised for the Long War stand on the stations they were raised at; the western seams are flooded and capped, and a pass is needed on the northern road. The Moot at Caol mhòr meets under Peter Hale with a grievance five years old, and the holdouts of no shire went out onto the windy coast. The Rite's twelve hewers cut four baskets of altar-coal from the last face of the Sloc Mòr, the Library keeps the war sealed, and the north keeps its Church and the telling of Naomh Breandan's voyage.

orders.name: Òrd Bhrìde
orders.name_en: the Coal Rite, the order of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone
orders.gods: Brìde; Crom Cruaich, the Monster of the Gates
orders.note: Given a settled doctrine in SE 6 and a high custodian, the Àrd-choimheadaiche, at the southern Seann Skell; it protests at the kingdom's use of the vein, and then blesses it.

orders.name: Òrd an t-Seabhaig
orders.name_en: the order of the Hawk of Acaill
orders.gods: Mòd, the Hungry Hawk; Fionntan mac Bòchra
orders.note: Refused the Rite's written order; named its own custodian at Inis ìseal and wrote its own order down; took a place under the high custodian keeping its order.

orders.name: Scoiltean nan Draoidhean
orders.note: Opened again when the vein began to fail; Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain lectures in Flidais's wood; a house at Caol shean.

orders.name: Òrd Mhacha
orders.name_en: the order of Macha, keeper of the regalia
orders.gods: Macha; the two horses of one yoke
orders.note: Crowned Niall by its rite and keeps the regalia; refused the Rite a share in the keeping.

orders.name: Òrd na Cloiche
orders.note: Its houses serve as banks as well as churches; sent the Rite a letter wishing it well.

orders.name: Òrd Mhanannain
orders.note: Says the lord of the sea has shut the eastern sea again; the house at Seann Bhral turned away the Tuathaich from its feast.

master.note: Warm springs below Muileann ruadh, whose water comes up out of the mountain at about a hundred and four degrees of the humans' scale. The sick have been bathed here since the Ancient Age for their ease and their healing, and the bath-house over the basins takes in the sick of every rite.

A holy stream in the east. It is told that whoever drinks of it in the right quarter of the moon will have good fortune, and pilgrims of every rite have walked to it since the Holy Age. Its water is clear as glass and carries a sheen of many colours that glints even in the dimmest light, and it is said never to have failed.

Muileann chiar, the silver town, stands beside the only silver seam on Dia-thìr, found in the Holy Age near the great vein and never part of it. The town's silver guild has held the seam ever since: against the Company in the Age of Strangers, and under the kingdom's charter now.
A stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, rebuilt and widened more than once on the same piers. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet.
An old stone crossing of the river above Ros fhionn, first built by Ailean Clachair, whose hearth-sign is still sharp in the keystone. Few have used it since the trade of the district fell away.

A great road-house of the old mining roads, and one of the best known. Its first keeper was Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean, and it still serves her jugged buffalo, with shiny water to drink. The War of the Roads was ended under its roof.

A great road-house on the eastern road, where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path. It faces south and is known for its warmth, for the songs of Fearchar Bàrd, and for pan-fried spinach with black wine, which it once set before the queen's progress.

A great road-house on the northern road above Inis mhòr, raised by Catrìona Ghlic for the carriers of the Hall's baskets. It serves oatcakes fried in linseed oil, with the barley spirit the carriers call fire water.

A great stone road-house on the bare moor of the northern road, built for carriers caught by the snow. Its fare is pickled spinach with fire milk; a party of reeves once lived on nothing else through a whole season snowed in.
A great road-house on the eastern road north of Seann Dunn, the first to be raised by a ruler's order, by Mòrag nan Rathad. It is known for syrupped beef, served with hot juice.

The great road-house at the halfway stage of the central mining road, where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the snow. The brothers Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn made their peace under its roof. It serves steamed carp with green brandy.

The far-off house on the eastern road near the silver country, so far from any town that carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway. The road-peace was first kept here, and no feud may be followed under its roof. Its fare is dried deer with black water.

The sea-light on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, the last of the five towers to be built. A fire was kept on this headland in the Ancient Age to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen; the tower is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

The sea-light on the eastern cape at Baile ìseal, the second of the five towers. The households of the coast kept a fire here in the Age of Ailean to bring the boats home in a storm, and the tower is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

The sea-light on the northern point at Muileann bheag, the fourth of the five towers and the first to burn coal. The ash of the old shore-fire lies three yards deep beneath it. It is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

The sea-light on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, the third of the five towers, marking the passage in toward Seann Tarr. Its keeper Tormod mac Pheadair kept a daybook of every ship he saw. It is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

The sea-light on the southern cape at Tobar dhearg, the first of the five towers. Here the island's first sea-light was raised above the ground, a stone tower with the fire on its top, and it is a beacon for ships in the open sea.
The field of the last great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War, fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22. The first and third regiments stood here, and the holdouts were broken.
The field of the first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War, fought on 11 an Giblean, DE 21. It has been left unploughed, and the Tuathaich have raised a cairn on it.

Toll-dubh, the western shaft of the Old Ones: cut straight down through the rock, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp can show, with no spoil heap beside it. Quarrymen from north of the capital broke into it in the Age of Sundering and found a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians walled the entrance up, and it has not been opened since.

Toll-dubh, the eastern shaft of the Old Ones, twin of the western one across the island. In the Age of Ailean a youth was let down into it on a rope of plaited hide and drawn up alive, and he never said what he had seen. Charcoal-burners found it again in the Age of Sundering, with the same cut stair as the western shaft, and the custodians walled it up. The people of Muileann ruadh keep away from it.

Uilebheist na Mara, the Sea-Watcher. Sailors have told of a great beast in these dangerous waters since the Ancient Age, and boats of Baile chrom have been lost here in a calm sea. Some say it is thirty feet long.

Marbh-bheò, the Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills. Old inscriptions there tell of a thing that walks without breath and falls on any who dare come near its lair or light a fire in its sight. No fire is lit where these hills can see it.
A forest sacred to Flidais, lady of the deer, where the druid schools, Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, keep their grove and her white stag is seen.
A forest sacred to Macha, where Òrd Mhacha keeps the wood of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse, yoke-fellow of Liath Macha, the Grey of Macha: the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night.

The raiders' water off the north-west coast. Outlaws put off in boats here in the Holy Age and lived by plundering the fishing strands, and raiders' ships have been seen in these waters in every age since.

The raiders' water off the east coast. Outlaws have raided the eastern strands from the islets offshore since the Holy Age. In the Age of Strangers they burned a Company coal ship here and ran rifles for the silver guild, and their low black boats are still seen.

The raiders' bays off Cathair gheal on the north-west coast. Raiders have taken the dried fish from these strands since the Holy Age. The fourth fleet found the bays empty after the Long War, but the fishermen say the raiders will be back.

An ancient obelisk. On its upper face runs a line in the script of the Old Ones, which no one can read; lower down, cut by a later hand with a narrower tool, are four words of Dia-thìris, Bha teine sa chloich, 'there was fire in the stone'.
An ancient pillar. It carries two words of Dia-thìris, Cuimhnich an teine, 'remember the fire', and round them signs in a script no one can read.

An ancient column. The people of Cnoc ghorm say it carries the doctrine of the Ancient Age, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann, 'we did not come; we were here'; the scholars who came to read it in the Holy Age could not.

Ruins of a walled outpost of the Old Ones on a spur above Cathair mhòr. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate faces inland and was blocked with rubble from the inside. Who built it is not known.

Ruins of a fortress of the Old Ones: three rings of wall and a cistern cut into the bedrock, with room for four hundred people and their beasts. It was long said to hold riches. The men of Baile ghorm who dug for them in the Holy Age found only ash, and the library's diggers found walls older than any Dia-thìrich building and no writing.

Ruins of a temple older than any faith on the island: a stepped platform of fitted stone whose altar is set square to the central mountains, not to the sea. Its top stone was prised off in the Ancient Age and has never been found. Edwin Lowe dug here for a season in the Age of Strangers and found cut stone, burnt bone and marks he could not read; the library has measured it and, at the asking of the district, left it undug.

The great library of Muileann chaol, founded in the Age of the Kingdom, with Ailean Leabhar for its first keeper. It holds the fullest record of the island's history that has come down, and many rare and ancient books. 'A chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute.

An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, the travelling circus that no one understands, pitched on the common near Inis àrsaidh. It stays only a little while and moves on. The magistrate who licensed it entered its acts as 'various'.

An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, the travelling circus that no one understands, where it was first seen, on the southern coast near Seann Chwen. It never stays long, and no one has yet said what its acts are meant to show.
The field of the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan. Fighters come from all over the island to its yearly melee, and men have died in it. The winner takes fame and fortune, and the crowd's favour.

The fair of Muileann òg, held at the ford where the Stone King Raghnall Ceannfhionn and the holder of the Red Hill agreed salt for wool, the oldest meeting-place on the island. Goods of Dia-thìr and of lands over the sea change hands here, and every craft and service is to be had.

Cidhe Beag, the little quay: an old landing on the Abhainn uaine, where boats have been put into the river since the Age of Ailean. A ferryman keeps it, a weary-looking man, and he will sell passage along the river.

Imrich nam Pantar, the panthers' crossing. The great cats' roads cross the mountains by the high passes and come down here, between Baile dhomhain and the southern Cnoc àrsaidh, over the southern road to the fens of the south-west coast, at the same season every year. The herders of the south-west keep the crossing days and drive their flocks off the paths beforehand.

Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the old burial ground on the hill, whose oldest graves are older than any name that can be read. The thorn grows back over the stones faster than the keepers can clear it, the flowers fade among them, and it is said that the dead walk there and mourn.

The moor above Cnoc naomh where the crew-leaders of the northern pits met in the spring before the Severance war and fixed the week of their rising. A cairn of spoil-stones from every pit that sent a man marks the place.

The standing stone on the moor road below Muileann dhomhain where the custodians of that town met the people turned out of the closed district of the Rending and lent them the land on which Achadh chaol was raised.
The stone on the neck of land between Caol chrom and Caol gharbh where the two harbours of the strait have met to settle its dues since the salt came to Caol gharbh in the Age of Sundering.

The water off the north-west cape where boats out of Achadh àrsaidh met the three ships coming down from the north in the first days of the Crossing and led them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishing boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow when they pass it.

The spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach where the keeper's stone cup and its three copies were first set side by side and filled from the spring, so that every hearth of the hills burned the coal by one measure.
Here, at Inis thais, the temple city of Òrd na Cloiche, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company, ended its road in the first spring of the Severance war.

Binnean a' Chlachair, the Mason's Point: the highest ground of Dia-thìr, a little under three thousand six hundred feet, on the bare moor above Muileann gheal in the Doire uaine hills. The Line of the Mason tells that Fearghas of that line carried the six unlit coals up here and let them fall, and that the coal flecked with white stars took fire in the air as it fell. The summit has borne the kindred's name since. Herders of Muileann gheal leave a stone on the top when they pass, and none will light a fire there.

polities.kingdom: The kingdom that the vein founded now runs on a fuel made by a Tuathach, and says so only in its coin. It fought its one war against its own people over the last coal of the west, and keeps the regiments it raised for it on their stations, paid from a tithe that was laid for the war and never lifted. Cathal reigns; the council keeps its twelve seats and one soldier.
polities.moot: The Moot meets at Caol mhòr under Peter Hale, great-grandson of its first speaker. It stood apart from the Long War and fed the hungry who came to its towns, and its motion for amends was allowed to die. Its minute-books run unbroken from Walter Hale's first meeting; its request that the Tuathaich tellings be kept in the Library still lies on the table.

burgs.19: Cathair dhearg, the red city, stands on the Red Hill, whose holders are named in the oldest king-lists; the old settlement shrank to a fishing town and grew again in the Holy Age where the mining roads came down to the water on the Abhainn dhomhain, just above Loch chrom, and Beathag Mhòr made it the seat of rule; Drochaid Cathair dhearg, heir of the first bridges, still carries the road across the river. It kept its walls, citadel and temple through the Sundering and the Age of Strangers, and after the Severance Rìoghachd Dia-thìr was declared here and Niall was crowned in it, first of the restored line. The royal precinct is small for a capital, ringed by the great harbours of Ros dhomhain, Cathair dhomhain and Baile ghlas, and its temple is the first house of Macha, where kings are made by her rite and the two horses of her rite, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black, are honoured. The royal quays build seagoing hulls for the Crown.
burgs.489: Seann Skell is the great river port of the west, a city of nearly twenty-eight thousand and, after the capital, the largest place on the island, whose barges run down the Abhainn naomh to Ros àrsaidh; its river harbour is a Seann-Dhaoine site and the name keeps their root. It is walled by its citadel rather than by curtain walls, and the seventh regiment, raised in the Long War, is stationed here. The first battle of that war was fought at Àth leathan, a short march north.
burgs.431: Seann Skell is the great southern port, a town of nearly twenty-three thousand whose harbour lies on a site the Seann-Dhaoine used before the Dia-thìrich; the name keeps their root. It is the seat of its province and a centre of Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame. The ninth regiment and the second fleet, raised in the Long War, are stationed here. It shares its name with the great western river port. Glass is blown there from the white sand of its own shore.
burgs.27: Ros dhomhain is the most populous place of the capital country, a merchant port that outgrew every wall it was ever given until no one built another. The first human traders lodged here after the Crossing, and its counting-houses have served every master of the island's trade since. It sits between the capital and the old harbour of Seann Vell, and the three have run together into one shore. The Company's railway, the coal line, came down to its deep-water quay from the pits at Muileann chrom in the years of Edward Vane's commission, and the first steamer seen on Dia-thìr had come into its harbour half a century before. In the present year its quay became the one place on the island where dubhan may be loaded for beyond the island, under the charter Dubhan won from the council: a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel, and the custodians of Brìde's order seal every hold.
burgs.95: Caol mhòr, the great strait, was a Dia-thìreach harbour from the Age of Ailean. After the Severance it became the chief port of the Tuathaich, and it is now their largest town. Its yards take timber from Doire mhin, and its people keep the faith of the Church.
burgs.246: A narrow mill town in the eastern hills, and the home of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the library that keeps the fullest record of the island. The library was founded in the new kingdom and has since taken in the provincial archives, and its war archive is sealed. The town lives on the library and on the river landing at Ceann dhomhain, and to put a thing in the Library is to settle it. Paper has been made here since the Age of Sundering, and its copyists and binders work for the library.
burgs.135: Achadh dhomhain of Muileann chrom is a large farming village in deep fields, founded in the Holy Age. Its granaries fed the mining camps in the Age of Strangers and were requisitioned in the war of the Severance. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha.
burgs.23: Cathair mhòr, the great city, grew from households of the Age of Ailean who settled below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, a Seann-Dhaoine outpost already in ruins, and it was walled in the Holy Age, the first walled town on the island. After the parting of the kingdom it was the seat of Eithne nic Ailein, the king's daughter, who held the lowland plain as one of the nine great shares and lived to swear the Peace of the Threshold. It commands the roads between the gulf and the vein country, and it was a counting-house of the tithe in the Age of Strangers and a mustering place in the war that ended it. An treas rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears its name. Its honey and its salted meat are sold in every market of the south, and its soap-boilers and weavers are the busiest in the gulf.
